title: Realism and Theory Change in Science

summaries.example: Imagine that children once used a map showing a mountain with a giant inside it. Later, a better map removes the giant but keeps the mountain’s shape and location. The old map was not completely right, yet it still helped people learn something. Philosophers ask whether scientific theories change in a similar way.
summaries.summary: Scientific theories sometimes become successful and widely accepted, then are changed or abandoned. This history creates a challenge for scientific realism, the view that successful theories can tell us about the real world, including things we cannot see. The pessimistic induction says that because many older theories turned out to be wrong, our current theories may also be replaced. Realist philosophers answer that theory change may include important kinds of continuity. Pierre Duhem distinguished a part that organizes observations from a part that explains them with hidden causes. He thought explanations may be discarded while useful descriptions and mathematical relationships remain. Henri Poincaré especially emphasized relationships between things. Ludwig Boltzmann argued that continuity might also include ideas about unseen entities, such as atoms. Later debates ask whether success really points to truth, whether some parts of old theories deserve trust more than others, and whether current science has any special advantage. The entry presents these arguments without treating the dispute as settled.
key_ideas: Science has changed many times, so some people wonder whether today’s theories will eventually be replaced too.
Some philosophers say that older theories may leave behind useful patterns, measurements, or relationships.
Duhem and Poincaré emphasized that mathematical relationships can survive changes in explanation.
Boltzmann argued that more than relationships might survive, including ideas about hidden things such as atoms.
The history of science can support both worry about science and hope that science is learning.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us think carefully about what scientific progress means. A theory can be useful without being completely correct, and a new theory can keep some valuable parts of an older one. It also teaches us not to jump from a list of past mistakes to the conclusion that all science is unreliable. We should ask what evidence a particular theory has and which parts of it do the important work.

important_terms.definition: The idea that science can tell us something about how the world really is, including things we cannot directly see.
The worry that because many older successful theories were replaced, today’s successful theories will also later be rejected.
The parts of a theory that describe patterns in what we observe, often with mathematics.
The proposed hidden causes or models used to explain what we observe.
The idea that some relationships or patterns can remain correct even when the objects used to explain them change.

questions_to_think_about: If an old theory is replaced, does that mean it was useless?
What might stay the same when scientists change an explanation?
Should a successful prediction make us believe a theory is true?
Why might scientists disagree about what part of an old theory was valuable?

summaries.example: Consider the change from Newton’s theory of gravity to Einstein’s general theory of relativity. Newtonian gravity was highly successful, including in calculating planetary motion, but it did not account for every observed detail. Einstein’s theory changed the framework while recovering important Newtonian results in an appropriate limiting case. This raises a central question: were the successful parts of Newton’s theory retained because they were approximately true, or can mathematical and predictive continuity be explained in another way?
summaries.summary: The entry examines whether scientific theory change threatens scientific realism. The historical record contains theories that were once successful and later rejected, motivating the pessimistic induction: if past successful theories failed, perhaps current successful theories will fail too. The challenge can target several realist commitments, including approximate truth, reference to unobservable entities, and the idea that success is explained by truthlikeness. Historical responses emphasize continuity rather than wholesale replacement. Duhem distinguishes a representative part of a theory, which organizes empirical laws mathematically, from an explanatory part involving models and hidden causes. He argues that representative content can survive while explanations are abandoned. Poincaré develops a related relationist position: mathematical relations may remain stable even when the entities or interpretations associated with them change. Boltzmann resists limiting continuity to relations and argues that retained theoretical elements, such as atoms, may also support realism. Contemporary selective realists use the divide et impera strategy: they distinguish success-producing theoretical commitments from idle or dispensable ones. Critics argue that this selection may be shaped by current beliefs, or that continuity does not by itself establish truthlikeness. Structural realism restricts realist commitment largely to mathematical structure. The entry also surveys disputes over whether the historical challenge is genuinely inductive, deductive, or better understood as a warrant-removing argument, and concludes that both detailed scientific evidence and broader historical evidence matter.
key_ideas: The historical challenge to realism begins with the record of successful theories later judged false or non-referring.
The challenge can be framed inductively, as a prediction about future theory change, or deductively, as an argument from counterexamples; each framing creates difficulties.
Duhem distinguished representative content from explanatory hypotheses, arguing that the former may persist when the latter are abandoned.
Poincaré defended continuity in mathematical relations, while Boltzmann allowed continuity to include theoretical entities and other retained elements.
Selective realists argue that empirical success does not support every claim in a theory equally; the claims that generate success may be retained by later theories.
Critics question whether apparent continuity is independently established or merely reconstructed from the standpoint of present theories.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate clarifies what it means to say that science progresses. Replacing a theory need not imply that every part of it was mistaken, but continuity must be demonstrated rather than simply assumed. The issue also reveals different levels of realist commitment: one may defend the existence of theoretical entities, only the relational structure represented by theories, or a selective set of claims that contributed to empirical success. Understanding these distinctions helps us evaluate scientific arguments without treating either past error or present success as decisive by itself.

important_terms.definition: The position that scientific theories aim to describe a mind-independent world and can be approximately true, including in claims about unobservable entities.
A history-based argument claiming that the repeated replacement of successful theories gives reason to expect current theories to be replaced as well.
The claim that theories become more accurate or more truthlike without necessarily becoming completely true.
An approach that separates the parts of an older theory responsible for its successes from less important assumptions, assigning realist commitment selectively.
The view that science gives knowledge primarily of mathematical or relational structure, rather than of the intrinsic nature of unobservable things.
The view that only relations among things are knowable, even if the underlying nature of those things exists.
A theory of reference according to which a theoretical term can continue referring to an entity across theory change because its reference is fixed through causal connections with phenomena.

A formal reformulation of a theory that replaces theoretical predicates with existentially quantified variables, preserving its observational consequences while avoiding direct use of theoretical terms.

questions_to_think_about: Does the existence of successful false theories undermine the connection between empirical success and truthlikeness, or only show that the connection is fallible?
What evidence would be needed to show that a past theory’s successful components were genuinely retained rather than merely redescribed?
Does structural realism provide a convincing middle position between full realism and instrumentalism?
Can the history of science give current theories an epistemic privilege, or does that require a quality-based comparison of particular cases?
How should first-order evidence for a theory be balanced against second-order evidence about the historical record of science?

summaries.example: Suppose a school uses a computer model to predict how water will move through a maze. The model makes good predictions, but its story about invisible “water runners” turns out to be wrong. A later model predicts the water even better and keeps some of the same equations. One student says the old model was basically a failure. Another says its equations captured real patterns. A third says even the invisible runners might have represented something real. This mirrors the disagreement about what survives when scientific theories change.
summaries.summary: The entry explores a problem for scientific realism: science has repeatedly replaced theories that once worked well. The pessimistic induction uses this record to argue that today’s successful theories may also be abandoned. The challenge is not simply that scientists sometimes make mistakes. It asks whether empirical success is a dependable sign that a theory is approximately true, especially when the theory discusses unobservable entities. Several responses focus on continuity. Pierre Duhem separates a theory’s representative part, which organizes experimental laws and mathematical relations, from its explanatory part, which proposes hidden mechanisms. He argues that later theories often preserve much of the representative part while rejecting older explanations. Henri Poincaré develops a related view in which relations between physical quantities can survive changes in how those quantities are interpreted. Ludwig Boltzmann offers a broader response: continuity may include theoretical entities, such as atoms, rather than only equations and relations. Modern realists use the divide et impera strategy. They argue that a successful theory may contain both important claims and dispensable assumptions, so the historical failure of some claims need not defeat realism about the claims retained and used in later theories. Critics respond that this selection may be influenced by present-day science and that preservation alone does not prove truth. Structural realism offers a more limited position, treating mathematical structure as the main object of scientific knowledge. The entry also considers whether the pessimistic argument is inductive or deductive and stresses the need to compare general historical evidence with the detailed evidence for particular theories.
key_ideas: The history of science includes influential theories that were successful for a time but later abandoned, creating a challenge for realism.
The pessimistic induction treats this history as evidence that present theories may have the same fate.
Duhem’s distinction suggests that mathematical descriptions and empirical laws may survive even when explanatory pictures disappear.
Poincaré focused on relations expressed in equations; Boltzmann argued that retained theoretical entities could also count as continuity.
Realists often respond selectively: a theory’s success may support only the parts that were actually important in producing that success.
Critics disagree about whether continuity leads to approximate truth and whether historians can identify successful parts independently of current theories.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters because it changes how we understand scientific progress and scientific humility. It is possible to recognize that old theories were partly successful without claiming that every part was true. The debate also gives us tools for separating predictions, mathematical structure, explanatory stories, and claims about hidden entities. Those distinctions help us judge both the achievements and the limits of science.

important_terms.definition: The view that successful science can give us knowledge about the world itself, including things that cannot be directly observed.
An argument from past theory changes: because successful older theories were later rejected, current theories may eventually be rejected too.
The part of a theory that organizes observations and experimental laws, often using mathematical relationships.
The part of a theory that proposes hidden causes, mechanisms, or models to explain observed events.
The idea that theories can change while some relationships between measurable quantities remain stable.
The strategy of separating the reliable, success-producing parts of a theory from assumptions that were not needed for its success.
The position that science can know the structure or relationships in the world without knowing the intrinsic nature of unobservable things.
The claim that a theory is closer to the truth than another theory, even though both may contain errors.

questions_to_think_about: Is a theory’s ability to make successful predictions enough reason to believe its hidden explanations?
When a new theory preserves an old equation, what exactly has been preserved?
Could an argument based on many failed theories be unfair if those theories are not a representative sample?
Does selecting the “good” parts of past theories genuinely answer the historical challenge?
What is the difference between knowing how things are related and knowing what things are made of?
